method.title: Who commutes in.
method.text: Census LODES (2023) links every job’s workplace block to the worker’s home block. Of 4.59 million New York City jobs, 1.23 million are held by people living outside the city within 150 km of Times Square. Another 170,000 held by people farther away are left out.

method.title: Households, not jobs.
method.text: Each tract’s NYC jobs become households by dividing by its workers per household (ACS 2020–24). A tract can’t send more households than it has.

method.title: Driving.
method.text: BTS LATCH (2017) estimates weekday household driving for every tract. It is annualised ×350.7 (261 weekdays, plus 104 weekend days at 86% of a weekday, from the 2017 NHTS), at EPA’s 400 g of CO₂ per mile. Transit commutes add EPA’s 0.093 kg per passenger-mile on the subway and 0.133 on commuter rail.

method.title: Home energy.
method.text: Each tract’s mix of detached houses, row houses and apartments (ACS) is multiplied by EIA RECS 2020 energy use by building type in the Middle Atlantic. Electricity uses eGRID 2023 regional rates; gas, oil and propane use EPA factors.

method.title: The blocked home.
method.text: An apartment in a building of five or more units on the NYC grid (3.0 t a year), plus the driving of the tracts where it would have been. Those are the car-light core (tracts where under 20% of workers drive), the tracts where homes have been added since 2015 (DCP Housing Database), or Staten Island with its own house mix.

method.title: Who’s priced out.
method.text: Eligible households commute to NYC jobs from outside the city, or from parts of it where at least 35% of workers drive, such as much of Staten Island, eastern Queens and southern Brooklyn. Priced-out households are drawn from each eligible tract in proportion to its households.

method.title: The priced-out share.
method.text: No study measures it directly, so it’s an adjustable assumption: 25% by default, with a plausible range of 10–40%. Mast (2023) traced who moved into 686 new market-rate buildings in 12 metros. In New York City, 8.2% of residents came straight from the suburbs, and the vacancies they left rippled outward until movers looked like the region as a whole. In Helsinki, chains of moves also end with newcomers from outside the region and with newly formed households (Bratu et al. 2023). Neither counts here.

method.title: The cost.
method.text: CO₂ cost = blocked homes × priced-out share × (household CO₂ where it lives now − CO₂ in a new NYC apartment). Tons are priced at $268, the charge NYC levies per ton over a building’s Local Law 97 cap.

limits: Who’s priced out is your choice on the panel, not a forecast.
The priced-out share is an assumption drawn from moving-chain research, not a measurement for New York City.
Blocked-homes counts are the city’s own estimates of what rule changes would allow, not measured counterfactuals.
A priced-out household keeps its size and income in the blocked home; in reality both can change.
LATCH models 2017 weekday driving on 2010 tracts. Split tracts take their parent’s value; 842 tracts that changed more take their county’s average.
LATCH has driving estimates for only 16 Manhattan tracts. The other Manhattan tracts use those tracts’ average, 6.8 miles a weekday.

Home energy uses regional averages by building type, not the actual building. New all-electric buildings under Local Law 154 likely use less than the RECS average, so the blocked-home figure is conservative.
eGRID rates cover power generated inside each grid region. NYC also imports cleaner upstate power, which would lower the city side.
Commute distances are straight lines between tract centres.
Embodied carbon from construction is left out. Every new home has it, wherever it’s built.
